author: Anwesha Ghosh
title: Municipal Calcutta: Urban Governance in a Colonial City
key_argument: The colonial Calcutta municipality was constitutively a corporation whose civic functions never displaced its profit motive; its ancestor is the EIC rent-collector ('Zemindar'), and 'municipal governmentality' fused benevolence with extraction.

author: Anwesha Ghosh
title: The Improvement Regime: Public Trusts, Real Estates, and India's Urban Futurities
key_argument: Comparing the Bombay and Calcutta improvement trusts, Ghosh argues the trust was constitutively designed to fail at sanitary housing while succeeding as the city's leading rentier via 'recoupment' (selling surplus land at future-speculative value) — a century-old 'improvement regime' prefiguring today's neoliberal urbanism.

author: Prashant Kidambi
title: Planning, the information order, and the Bombay census of 1901
key_argument: The 1890s plague crisis triggered the colonial state to create the Bombay Improvement Trust (1898) as a new planning agency and to overhaul its 'information order' (the 1901 census) — the planning-agency carve-out Ghosh builds on. Kidambi's broader work (The Making of an Indian Metropolis) on the BIT and 'housing the poor' is the keystone Bombay reference Ghosh cites.

author: Stephen Legg
title: Post-Colonial Developmentalities: From the Delhi Improvement Trust to the Delhi Development Authority
relation_to_Ghosh: parallels / extends across the colonial-postcolonial divide
key_argument: Traces the institutional continuity from the Delhi Improvement Trust (1937/38) to the Delhi Development Authority — the exact colonial-to-postcolonial lineage of the unelected planning body that Ghosh's frame names; shows the DDA inherited the trust's land-and-congestion logic.

author: Stephen Legg
title: Prostitution and the Ends of Empire: Scale, Governmentalities, and Interwar India
key_argument: Develops scaled colonial governmentality in interwar India; methodologically adjacent to Ghosh's 'municipal governmentality' and her argument that the municipality produced 'the local' as a scale of rule.

author: Awadhendra Sharan
title: From source to sink: 'Official' and 'improved' water in Delhi, 1868-1956
key_argument: Reads the making of colonial Delhi through the rhetoric of 'improvement' and 'progress' applied to water and purity — the same improvement-language Ghosh anatomises, in the water register.

author: Ravi Sundaram
title: Pirate Modernity: Delhi's Media Urbanism
relation_to_Ghosh: contrasts (bottom-up to Ghosh's top-down institutional reading)
key_argument: Charts Delhi from 1950s technocratic planning through the post-1977 expansions to the 1990s urban crisis, theorising 'pirate modernity' — the non-legal media/urban life that exceeds the planned city; a counterpoint to Ghosh's institution-centred account.

author: Debjani Bhattacharyya
title: Empire and Ecology in the Bengal Delta: The Making of Calcutta
key_argument: Shows how colonial law dried Calcutta's 'soaking ecologies' into registered, speculable property — the property-making and dispossession that underpins Ghosh's account of the municipality making and seizing land.

author: Debjani Bhattacharyya
title: A River Is Not a Pendulum: Sediments of Science in the World of Tides
key_argument: On the colonial scientific management of Calcutta's tidal/riverine environment; extends her property-and-ecology argument that Ghosh draws on.

author: Prashant Kidambi (Anwesha Ghosh, via)
title: Housing the Poor in a Colonial City: The Bombay Improvement Trust, 1898-1918
key_argument: Documents the BIT's failure to rehouse the poor it displaced — the 'failure' reading that Ghosh's 'Improvement Regime' reframes as constitutive design rather than incompetence. (Cited within Ghosh and McGowan; not held as a standalone Zotero record.)

author: Nikhil Anand
title: Hydraulic City: Water and the Infrastructures of Citizenship in Mumbai
key_argument: Water infrastructure produces differentiated 'hydraulic citizenship'; Mumbai's colonial-era water system was built to support only a 'limited liberal governance', serving some subjects and abandoning others — the fractured public, in pipes.

author: Nikhil Anand
title: PRESSURE: The PoliTechnics of Water Supply in Mumbai
key_argument: Settlers mobilise the 'pressure' of politics, pumps and pipes to claim water the state neglects to deliver; the water department (est. 1860) is shown as a selective, politically mediated provider.

author: Nikhil Anand
title: Municipal disconnect: On abject water and its urban infrastructures
key_argument: Examines how some residents and spaces are rendered 'abject' and disconnected from municipal water — uneven provision as a governing technique.

author: Nikhil Anand
title: Leaky States: Water Audits, Ignorance, and the Politics of Infrastructure
key_argument: Water audits and the production of official 'ignorance' about leakage are political technologies — the technocratic measurement of water as governance, echoing Ghosh's 'trusting the experts'.

author: Nikhil Anand
title: Consuming Citizenship: Prepaid Meters and the Politics of Technology in Mumbai
key_argument: Prepaid water meters recast the citizen as a paying consumer — the market-governance logic Ghosh traces to colonial Calcutta, in a 21st-century device.

author: Zainab Bawa
title: Where is the State? How is the State? Accessing Water and the State in Mumbai and Johannesburg
key_argument: The organisational form of the water utility and councillors' proximity to decision-makers shape who can access piped water — an institutional-mediation account of the elected councillor's limited reach, resonant with Ghosh's power-map.

author: Sapana Doshi
title: The Redevelopmental State: Governing Surplus Life and Land in the 'Urban Age'
key_argument: Theorises the 'redevelopmental state' that sutures ethno-religious nationalism, urbanised accumulation and populist welfare to manage land dispossession in Mumbai — the contemporary descendant of Ghosh's recoupment regime.

author: Juned Shaikh
title: Outcaste Bombay: City Making and the Politics of the Poor
key_argument: Documents the symbiosis of industrial capitalism and caste in 20th-century Bombay, where planners marked Dalit neighbourhoods as slums to be demolished for a 'modern' city — caste as the axis of who the 'improvement' machine displaces.

author: Karen Coelho
title: Of Engineers, Rationalities, and Rule: An Ethnography of Neoliberal Reform in an Urban Water Utility in South India
key_argument: An ethnography of Chennai Metrowater under neoliberal reform: audit culture and commensuration empower accountants over engineers and harden hostility toward 'over-politicized' slum-dwellers — the technocratic, depoliticised utility Ghosh's 'trusting the experts' predicts.

author: Nityanand Jayaraman, Lindsay Bremner, Karen Coelho, Pooja Kumar, Saravanan Kasinathan
title: Counter-Mapping, Counter-Histories, and Insurgencies of Subjugated Knowledges in the Fisher Struggle for Ennore Creek
key_argument: Fisher communities' counter-maps of Ennore Creek contest the state's industrial land-use claims — a method of resistance to the improvement/development logic Ghosh describes.

author: Niranjana R.
title: Between Fragments and Ordering: Engineering Water Infrastructures in a Postcolonial City
key_argument: Chennai's Metrowater grid is a patchwork of fragmentary engineering epistemologies, not a singular will to order — complicating the technocratic coherence the improvement regime claims.

author: Catriona Ellis
title: 'If You Cannot Feed the Body of a Child You Cannot Feed the Brain': Education and Nutrition in Late Colonial Madras
key_argument: The Madras Municipal Corporation's 1925 midday-meals scheme shows an elected, relatively autonomous local body pursuing welfare — a partial counter-case to the purely extractive municipality, useful for testing the limits of Ghosh's frame.

author: Bhavani Raman
title: Document Raj: Writing and Scribes in Early Colonial South India
key_argument: Petitioning and paperwork made ordinary Madras inhabitants into juridical subjects of Company rule — the documentary statecraft underlying the 'property making and taking' Ghosh foregrounds. (Ghosh draws on Raman for the law-as-groundwork-for-dispossession move.)

author: R. E. Frykenberg
title: On Roads and Riots in Tinnevelly: Radical Change and Ideology in Madras Presidency during the 19th Century
key_argument: Riots erupted over making roads and facilities 'public' in 19th-century Madras Presidency — the contested making of 'the public' that Ghosh's 'fractured public' theorises.

author: Aparna Balachandran
title: Petitions, the City, and the Early Colonial Public in Madras
key_argument: On the Madras corporation as an early experiment in urban governance and the 'trader-governor' — the precedent Ghosh explicitly invokes for reading a municipal government as a corporation. (Named in Ghosh's frame; not held as a standalone Zotero record in this corpus.)

author: Janaki Nair
title: The Promise of the Metropolis: Bangalore's Twentieth Century
key_argument: The definitive 20th-century history of Bangalore's making — planning, public space, industry and the politics of a metropolis; the planning-and-power backdrop against which Goldman's speculative urbanism is read.

author: Carol Upadhya
title: Imagining India: Software and the Ideology of Liberalisation
key_argument: Bangalore's IT capitalist class positions itself as leader of the 'new India', driving land and urban-development conflicts that exclude large sections of the population — the contemporary corporate capture of the city.

author: Hemangini Gupta
title: Experimental Times: Startup Capitalism and Feminist Futures in India
key_argument: Ethnography of Bengaluru's transformation into a speculative 'Startup India' city, where state officials and entrepreneurs orient toward an imagined innovation future — futurity as governance, Ghosh's 'rendering the future available in the present' in startup form.

author: Vinay Gidwani & Rajyashree N. Reddy
title: The Afterlives of 'Waste': Notes from India for a Minor History of Capitalist Surplus
key_argument: 'Wastelands' become the new frontier of accumulation for Bangalore's knowledge economy via 'eviscerating urbanism' — the colonial 'waste' category Ghosh's improvement regime also weaponises, traced into the present.

author: Nafis Aziz Hasan
title: Citizen Labor
key_argument: Digitisation of Karnataka land records (Bhoomi) shifts the labour of maintaining property data onto citizens, degrading substantive citizenship — property-making as governance, now digital.

author: Shreyas Sreenath
title: Numbing Machines
key_argument: Post-abolition manual scavenging persists in Bengaluru's sewers through contractualisation that 'instrumentalises untouchable bodies' — caste power calibrated through urban sanitation infrastructure.

author: Michael Goldman
title: Speculative Urbanism and the Making of the Next World City (Bangalore)
key_argument: Coins 'speculative urbanism': the Bangalore state and global finance speculate on a future 'world city', dispossessing land and reorganising governance around anticipated value — the direct contemporary analogue of Ghosh's land-futurity regime. (Repeatedly cited within the corpus, e.g. Hasan and Doshi, as 'Goldman 2011/2020'; Goldman's own articles are not held as standalone Zotero records here.)

author: Sangeeta Kamat
title: Neoliberalism, Urbanism and the Education Economy: Producing Hyderabad as a 'Global City'
key_argument: Hyderabad is remade as an IT 'global city' through educational restructuring and the creation of the Hyderabad Metropolitan Development Authority — a new parastatal that redraws city boundaries to serve globally mobile populations while neglecting established communities; the development-authority carve-out, Telangana edition.

author: Mona G. Mehta
title: Ahmedabad: The Middle Class Megacity
key_argument: Ahmedabad's middle class drives an exclusionary 'Megacity' project that lets it realise political interests without depending on electoral democracy — the bypassing of the elected city Ghosh's depoliticisation thesis anticipates, in the Gujarat-model register.

author: Arvind Rajagopal
title: Special Political Zone: Urban Planning, Spatial Segregation and the Infrastructure of Violence in Ahmedabad
key_argument: Ahmedabad's urban planning (back to Geddes) and spatial practices ghettoised Muslims and produced an 'infrastructure of violence' — improvement/planning as a technology of communal segregation.

author: Abigail McGowan
title: Ahmedabad's Home Remedies: Housing in the Re-Making of an Industrial City, 1920-1960
key_argument: When Indians took control of Ahmedabad's urban politics from the 1920s, housing became a vehicle for a briefly inclusive vision of the city — before the 1950s retreat into class and community segregation; a more agentive municipal history than the extractive default.

author: Rakib Akhtar
title: 'Development Has Gone Crazy': The Gujarat Model of 'Unequal' Development through Neoliberalism and Hindutva
key_argument: The Gujarat model fuses Hindutva and neoliberalism to produce unequal development across class, caste and religion — the political economy in which Ahmedabad's unelected, growth-first urban governance operates.

author: Abigail McGowan
title: Khadi Curtains and Swadeshi Bed Covers: Textiles and the Changing Possibilities of Home in Western India, 1900-1960
key_argument: Plague-era sanitary intervention by the Bombay Improvement Trust reshaped the western-Indian home and ideas of comfort and privacy — the BIT's reach into domestic life, a fine-grained companion to Kidambi and Ghosh.

author: Michael Levien
title: Dispossession without Development: Land Grabs in Neoliberal India
key_argument: Post-liberalisation Indian states became 'land broker states', dispossessing land for rent-heavy private real estate rather than labour-absorbing industry — the recoupment logic generalised to the national land regime.

author: Carol Upadhya
title: Assembling Amaravati: Speculative Accumulation in a New Indian City
key_argument: The building of Amaravati as a greenfield capital ran on speculative land pooling and accumulation — the purest contemporary instance of governing through land futurity, Ghosh's recoupment at city-founding scale.

author: Nabaparna Ghosh
title: A Hygienic City-Nation: Space, Community, and Everyday Life in Colonial Calcutta
key_argument: Calcutta's upper-caste bhadralok performed 'civicization', folding colonial health-and-sanitation rhetoric into caste and purity norms — the caste underside of municipal 'improvement' that Anwesha Ghosh cites but does not centre. (Cited in Ghosh 2025; not held as a standalone Zotero record in this corpus.)

author: Partho Datta
title: Planning the City: Urbanization and Reform in Calcutta, c. 1800-c. 1940
key_argument: The standard history of Calcutta's planning and the CIT, source of Ghosh's recoupment genealogy (Lottery Committee 1817) and her devolution-as-travesty quotation ('foist the costs of government to the local populace in the name of devolution'). (Cited extensively by Ghosh; not held as a standalone Zotero record in this corpus.)
